body.x: Temporary marriage — mut'ah, in Arabic — is among the most argued-about topics in Islamic law and one of the least calmly explained. Twelver Shia fiqh recognises it as a valid form of marriage contract; the Sunni schools do not. This page explains, without advocacy in either direction, what the contract is in Shia law, the conditions that make it valid, the rights and limits it creates, and the sensitivities that surround it in real communities. It ends with a clarity that matters to us: Shia Rishta is a platform for permanent nikah only, and nothing here treats this contract as something casual.

In Shia law, mut'ah is a marriage concluded for a fixed, stated period — which may be short or long — in return for a specified mahr. Shia scholars rest its permissibility on verse 24 of Surah an-Nisa, as read in their tradition, together with the practice of the earliest period, and hold that it was never validly abrogated; Sunni scholars read the evidence differently, as the next sections note. Within Shia fiqh it is not a licence and not an informal arrangement. It is a contract with the same seriousness of form as permanent marriage: an offer and an acceptance recited in the seegha, the free consent of both parties, and — for a woman who has never been married — the same guardian-permission rules that the majority of marjas apply to permanent nikah.
The conditions that make it valid
The manuals set out conditions for the contract. These are the core of them:

A fixed duration, stated in the contract itself — a day, a year, ninety-nine years. If no duration is specified, the contract is not a valid temporary marriage.
A specified mahr, agreed beforehand. Unlike permanent nikah, where an unstated mahr is later settled by a customary equivalent, a temporary contract concluded without a stated mahr is void.
The seegha recited correctly, by the couple themselves or by representatives they have authorised.
The free consent of both parties, and the wali's permission in the cases where the rules require it.
No legal impediment — neither party may be in an existing marriage or a waiting period that bars this contract.

Because the duration and the mahr are pillars of this contract rather than details, scholars insist both be unambiguous before the seegha is recited. Vagueness that a permanent contract might survive, this one does not.
Rights, limits and the waiting period

The default rules differ from permanent marriage in ways anyone considering the question must know beforehand. The spouses do not automatically inherit from one another, though inheritance can be written in as a condition. The husband is not automatically obliged to provide maintenance unless that, too, is stipulated. Other conditions can likewise be written into the contract by mutual agreement — where the parties will live, for instance, or that maintenance will be provided after all — and a condition lawfully agreed becomes binding on both sides for the contract's duration. There is no divorce in a temporary marriage: it ends when the term expires, or earlier if the husband gifts the remaining time to the wife, and the couple may also renew the arrangement or replace it with a permanent contract. Any child born of the marriage is fully legitimate, with the same lineage, rights and claim on both parents as a child of permanent marriage — on this point there is no dispute. When the contract ends, the woman observes iddah before any new marriage: the standard ruling is two complete menstrual cycles, or forty-five days for a woman who does not menstruate, and until delivery if she is pregnant.

The four Sunni schools hold temporary marriage to be prohibited and invalid, on the basis of reports that the Prophet forbade it after an early period in which it had been permitted. The Shia position is that those reports do not establish an abrogation of the Quranic verse. This is a genuine, centuries-old scholarly disagreement, and a page like this one is not going to settle it. What matters practically is honesty: a contract that one community recognises and another does not should never be presented to a partner, a family or a registrar as something it is not.

Whatever its status in the law books, mut'ah carries heavy social sensitivity in most Shia communities, where it is widely viewed with suspicion and associated in the public mind with secrecy and exploitation — concerns scholars themselves voice when they warn against arrangements hidden from families or leaving women unprotected. A woman who enters such a contract may find her reputation, and her future prospects of permanent marriage, judged by standards the law books do not set. Families are rarely involved, community recognition is limited, and the civil law of most countries gives the contract no standing at all. Anyone weighing the question seriously should discuss it openly with a qualified scholar, and should weigh the social cost with the same honesty as the legal ruling.
A clear note from Shia Rishta

Shia Rishta exists for one purpose: permanent nikah, entered with lifelong intent, family knowledge and community blessing. We do not offer, arrange or facilitate temporary marriage, and profiles or messages seeking it are removed. This guide exists because seekers ask factual questions and deserve factual answers — the same reason a map shows roads it does not recommend travelling. For either contract, your marja and a qualified scholar are the authorities; this page is information, not a ruling.

excerpt: Mut'ah — temporary marriage in Twelver Shia fiqh — explained factually: its conditions, its rules on mahr, duration and iddah, the Sunni position, and the social sensitivities around it.
title: Temporary nikah in Islam: rules explained
